Meccan, except for six verses, namely: ﴿These two adversaries...﴾ up to ﴿...to the path of the Praiseworthy﴾. It has seventy-eight verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

The zalzalah (violent shaking and disturbance) is the intense agitation and upheaval, and the doubling of the slipping of things [[His words "and the doubling of the slipping of things" mean the repeated deviation of things and their displacement from their places. In al-Sihah: "One says zallalta, O so-and-so (with a fatḥah), tazillu zalīlan, when one slips in mud or in speech." (ʿ)]] from their stations and their centres. The Hour may be either the agent of the shaking, as if it were itself what shakes things, by way of the figurative attribution (al-majāz al-ḥukmī), so that zalzalah is a verbal noun attributed to its agent; or the object of the shaking, in the manner of the extension in the adverb of time (al-ittisāʿ fī al-ẓarf) and treating it as a direct object, as in His words ﴿Nay, but it was your plotting by night and day﴾. It is the same shaking mentioned in His words ﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) convulsion﴾.

The time of it is disputed. Al-Ḥasan said it will occur on the Day of Resurrection, while ʿAlqamah and al-Shaʿbī said it will occur at the rising of the sun from its west.

He commanded the children of Adam to be mindful of Allah, then gave the reason for its obligation upon them by mentioning the Hour and describing it with the most terrifying description, so that they might look upon that description with their insight, imagine it with their intellects, and thus protect themselves and spare themselves from the hardships of that day, by complying with what their Lord commanded them: to clothe themselves in the garment of taqwā, which does not secure them from those terrors unless they clothe themselves with it.

It is narrated that these two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited them, and that night he did not see more weeping than that night. When they woke in the morning, they did not unsaddle the mounts, did not pitch the tents at the time of halting, and did not cook in any pot, and they were among the sorrowful, the weeping, and the pensive. [[Thus al-Tha'labī and al-Baghawī mentioned it. They both said: It is narrated from ʿImrān ibn Ḥuṣayn, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, and others that these two verses were revealed at night during the expedition of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, to the end." I say: It is a composite of the two narrations mentioned. The third is Ibn ʿAbbās, as narrated by Ibn Isḥāq from al-Kalbī from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said: "While the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was on his journey in the expedition of Banū al-Muṣṭaliq, there was revealed upon him ﴿O mankind, fear your Lord﴾ up to ﴿severe﴾. **Yawma tarawnaha** (﻿﴿on the Day you see it﴾)

This is in the accusative case, governed by *tadhhalu* (﴿will be distracted﴾). The pronoun refers to *al-zalzala* (the quaking).

*Wa-tadhhalu kullu murdi'atin* (﴿every nursing mother will be distracted﴾) is also read with the verb in the passive form, *tudhhalu kullu murdi'atin*, meaning: *tudhhiluha al-zalzala* (the quaking will distract her). *Al-dhuhul* (distraction, a term meaning to be diverted from a matter by astonishment) is leaving something aside together with bewilderment.

If you ask why it says *murdi'a* (nursing mother) and not *mur'ith* (a woman who nurses): *al-murdi'a* is the woman who is in the act of nursing, having put her breast to the infant's mouth. *Al-mur'ith* is one whose nature is to nurse, even if she is not actually nursing at the time described. [[Mahmud said: "*Mur'ith* is used as a relative adjective (*nisba*), while *murdi'a* is based on the original form of the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*)." Ahmad said: The difference between them is that when the word comes in the relative form, the occurrence of the attribute from which it is derived is not implied; rather, it means that she is characterized by it. In the non-relative form, the occurrence of the action and the attribute's emergence from it is implied. This is also the case in the verse, since God says ﴿what she nursed﴾, so He brought the attribute in the form of the action and added the feminine *ta'*.]] So it says *murdi'a*, to show that when this terror overtakes her while she has put the infant to her breast, she pulls him away from her mouth because of the astonishment that befalls her, ﴿from what she nursed﴾, meaning from her nursing, or from the one she nursed, who is the child.

Al-Hasan said: ﴿the nursing mother is distracted from her child before weaning, and the pregnant woman casts down her burden before its completion﴾.

It is read *wa-taraa* with a *damma* (vowel on the *ta'*), from *ariituka qa'iman* (I showed you standing) or *ru'yatuka qa'iman* (your seeing [someone] standing).

**Wa-l-nas** (﴿and the people﴾) is read in the accusative and in the nominative. The accusative is clear. If one reads it in the nominative, *al-nas* is the subject of *tara*, and the verb is made feminine according to the interpretation of it as a collective.

It is read *sukara*, which is parallel to *jau'a* and *atsha* (hungry, thirsty) for *ju'an* and *atshan* (hungry, thirsty). *Sukara* and *bi-sukara* (drunk) are like *kusali* and *ajali* (lazy, hasty). Al-A'mash read *sukra* and *bi-sukra* with a *damma*, which is unusual. The meaning is: ﴿and you see them as drunk﴾, by way of comparison (*tashbih*), ﴿and they are not drunk﴾ in reality.

[[Mahmud said: "His saying ﴿and you see the people as drunk, and they are not drunk﴾ first affirms for them a figurative drunkenness (*al-sukr al-majazi*), then negates real drunkenness." Ahmad said: The scholars say that one of the indicators of figurative usage (*majaz*) is that its opposite is true. As when you say "Zayd is a donkey" to describe his stupidity, then it is also true to say "he is not a donkey," thereby negating the literal sense. Likewise in the verse, after affirming figurative drunkenness, it negates the literal sense with the most emphatic negation, reinforced by the *ba'*. The reason for this emphasis is to alert that this drunkenness they have in that state is not like anything known; it is a matter they had never experienced before. The corrective (*istidrak*) in His saying ﴿but the punishment of God is severe﴾ refers back to His saying ﴿and they are not drunk﴾. It is as if it were a justification for affirming figurative drunkenness, as though it were said: "If they are not drunk from wine, which is the known drunkenness, then what is this strange drunkenness and what is its cause?" So it answers: its cause is the severity of God's punishment. It is related from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: it is the time when each of the prophets, upon them be peace and blessings, says, "Myself! Myself!"]] But what overtakes them of fear of God's punishment is what removes their minds and disperses their discernment, and returns them to a state like that of one whose intellect and discernment have been taken by drunkenness. It has also been said: ﴿and you see them as drunk﴾ from fear, ﴿and they are not drunk﴾ from wine.

If you ask why it first says *tarawna* (you see, plural) and then *tara* (you see, singular): the seeing was first attached to the quaking, so that all the people became seers of it. Then it is finally attached to the people being in the state of drunkenness, so each one of them must be made a seer of all the others.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verses 3–4:

It has been said: it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who was a disputatious man and would say: "The angels are daughters of God," "the Qur'an is the fables of the ancients," and "God is not able to revive one who has decayed and become dust." The verse is general, covering everyone who engages in disputation about what is permissible for God and what is not, regarding His attributes and actions, who does not refer to knowledge and does not bite down on it with a decisive molar, and in whom there is no following of proof nor submission to fairness. He gropes blindly like a night-blinded camel, not distinguishing between truth and falsehood. ﴿And he follows every rebellious devil﴾ (22:3), whose condition is known, manifest and clear, that whoever takes him as a guardian, his guardianship yields nothing but leading him astray from the path of Paradise and guiding him to the Fire.

[[The phrase "the leaders of the people of desires" (ru'asa' ahl al-ahwa'), if he means Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna), as is his habit in writing, reviling them, then he should be asked to differentiate between them and the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school), since they deserve the reviling rather than them. (ʿ)]] And I see the leaders of the people of desires, innovations, and the Hashwiyya (literalist traditionalists, a term used polemically), who claim the title of imam in the religion of God, are none other than those who fall first and directly under all of this. Rather, they are the most misleading of the devils and the most cutting off of the path of truth, in that they have codified error in writing and instilled it in their followers by rote, as if they had mixed it with their flesh and their blood. It is about them that one said:

"O, many a one whose steps are followed among his people, / a path of salvation, in their view, straight and clear, is a way..."

[[Yā is either for alerting or for calling, and the one being called is omitted. Al-maqfuww: the one who is followed. Al-khuṭā: plural of khuṭwa (step), used figuratively for actions, in that both share following in each. Likewise, al-ṭarīq (the path) is used figuratively for "being followed," in terms of his being followed in them and persisting in them. Mustawī: straight. Al-nahj, al-minhaj and al-minhāj: the clear path. Al-i'wijāj (crookedness) is used figuratively for confusion and for lying. ʿAjjū: they clamored and shouted.]]

"O God, keep us firm upon the correct creed which You have approved for Your angels in Your heavens and for Your prophets on Your earth, and admit us by Your mercy among Your righteous servants."

"And the writing upon him is an analogy, i.e., it is as if the one who takes him as a guardian has had his misguidance written against him and marked by it, because of its manifestation in his condition." It has been read as *annahu* and *fa-annahu*, with both fatha and kasra. Whoever reads with fatha: the first (*annahu*) is the object of *kutiba* (it was written), and the second is conjoined to it. Whoever reads with kasra: it is by way of quoting what was written verbatim, as if this statement was written upon him, just as you say: "I wrote: Indeed God is the Self-Sufficient, the Praiseworthy." Or it is taken as if there is an implied "it was said." Or because *kataba* carries the meaning of saying.

[[His saying "huwa ka-annamā" is perhaps: i.e., ka-annamā. (ʿ)]]

Al-Hasan read ﴿مِنَ الْبَعْثِ﴾ with a vowel on the first letter (*min al-ba'th*, "from the resurrection"). Its counterpart is *al-jalb* and *al-ṭard* in ﴿فِي الْجَلْبِ وَالطَّرْدِ﴾, as if it had been said: if you doubt the resurrection, what removes your doubt is that you look into the beginning of your creation. *Al-'alaqah* is a clot of congealed blood.

*Al-mudghah* is a small piece of flesh, the amount that can be chewed. *Al-mukhallaqah* is that which is shaped and smooth, free of deficiency and defect. It is said: "He shaped (*khalaqa*) the *siwāk* and the stick," when he trimmed and smoothed it, from their saying "a smooth (*khalqā'*) rock," when it is smooth. It is as if God, exalted is He, creates the lumps of flesh in varying states: some of them are complete in form, smooth and free of defects, and others are the opposite. Following this variation comes the variation among people in their make, their forms, their height and shortness, and their completeness and deficiency.

﴿Then We bring you forth as infants﴾ and ﴿from one state to another and from one form to another﴾ are so that We may make Our power and wisdom clear to you through this gradual process, and that He who is able to create man first from dust, then from a drop (*nuṭfah*) of semen, with no proportion between water and dust, is able to turn the drop into a clot, though there is a manifest difference between them, and then turn the clot into a lump, and the lump into bones. Such a one is able to restore what He originated, indeed this is more within His power than that, and easier by analogy. The verb in its intransitive form (*ghayr muʻaddā*), without an object for the verb *yubayyin* ("make clear"), is an announcement that through these acts there becomes clear of His power and knowledge what no mention can encompass and no description can comprehend.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah read ﴿لِيُبَيِّنَ لَكُمْ﴾ (*li-yubayyina lakum*, with the verb in the third person). ﴿وَنُقِرُّ﴾ (*wa-nuqirru*) with the ya' (*yaqirru*) is also read. It is also read *wa-nuqirru*. And ﴿وَنُخْرِجُكُمْ﴾ (*wa-nukhrijukum*) with the nun and the accusative. *Yaqirru* and *yukhrijukum* ("yuqirru, yukhrijukum"): with the accusative and the nominative. From Ya'qub: *nuqirru*, with the nun and a ḍammah on the qaf, from *qarra al-māʼ* when he poured the water. So the reading with the nominative (*raf'*) is a statement that He settles in the wombs whatever He wills to settle of that until a named term, which is the time of delivery, the end of six months, or nine, or two years, or four, or as He wills and decrees. Whatever He does not will to settle, the wombs eject or miscarry. The reading with the accusative (*naṣb*) is a causal clause coordinated with another causal clause.

Its meaning: We created you developing in this gradual manner for two purposes. The first: that We make Our power clear. The second: that We settle in the wombs whom We settle, until they are born, grow up, reach the limit of legal responsibility, and then I impose obligations upon them. This reading is supported by His words ﴿ثُمَّ لِتَبْلُغُوا أَشُدَّكُمْ﴾ (*thumma li-tablughū ashuddakum*, "then that you may reach your maturity"), in the plural, because the aim is to indicate the species. It may also mean: We bring out each one of you as a child. *Al-ashudd* is the full completion of strength, intellect and discernment. It is one of the plural forms for which no singular has been used, like *al-asaddah*, *al-qutūd* and *al-abāṭīl*, and as if they denote severity in more than one thing, so they were formed on the plural pattern for that reason. [[His words "one of the plural forms for which no singular has been used, like *al-asaddah*, *al-qutūd* and *al-abāṭīl*": what is in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* is that *al-sadd*, with a fatḥah, is the singular of *al-asaddah*, which means defects. Those are like blindness, deafness and muteness, contrary to analogy, and its analogical form would have been *sudūd*. *Al-qatad* is the wooden frame of a saddle, and its plural is *qutūd* and *aqtād*. *Al-bāṭil* is the opposite of truth, and its plural is *abāṭīl*, contrary to analogy, as if they had pluralized *abṭīl*. In it also is His words, exalted is He, ﴿حَتَّى يَبْلُغَ أَشُدَّهُ﴾ (*ḥattā yablugha ashuddahu*, "until he reaches his maturity"), i.e. his strength, which is a singular that came in the pattern of a plural, like *ānuk*, which is lead, and there is no parallel to these two. It is called a plural having no singular from its own form, like *abābīl*, *ʻabādīd* and *madhākīr*. (ʻ)]] Read: ﴿وَمِنكُم مَّن يُتَوَفَّىٰ﴾ (*wa-minkum man yutawaffā*, "and among you is he who is taken in death"), i.e. God takes him, ﴿إِلَىٰ أَرْذَلِ الْعُمُرِ﴾ (*ilā arhadhil-ʻumr*, "to the most abject age"), senility and dotage, until he returns to his first state of childhood: weak in constitution, feeble in intellect, poor in understanding. This shows that just as He is able to raise him through stages of increase until he reaches full completion, He is able to bring him down until he ends in the lowest state, ﴿لِكَيْلَا يَعْلَمَ مِن بَعْدِ عِلْمٍ شَيْئًا﴾ (*li-kaylā yaʻlama min baʻdi ʻilmin shay'ā*, "so that he knows nothing after having known"). That is, he becomes such that if he acquires knowledge of something he is quick to forget it, and his knowledge slips away from him, so that he asks about it at once. He says to you, "Who is this?" and you say, "So-and-so," and he does not wait a moment before asking you about it again.

Abu 'Amr read *al-ʻumr* with the mim sukun. *Al-hāmidah* is the dead, dried-up thing. This is a second proof of resurrection, and because it is evident and observed directly, God repeated it in His Book: ﴿اهْتَزَّتْ وَرَبَتْ﴾ (*ihtazzat wa-rabat*, "it stirs and swells"), i.e. it moves with plants and swells. It was also read *rabʼat*, i.e. it rose. *Al-bahīj* is the beautiful thing that is pleasing to the one who looks at it.

That is: the things We have mentioned—the creation of the children of Adam and the giving of life to the earth, together with the various kinds of wisdom and subtle purposes contained within them—come about through this, and this is the cause of their occurrence; without it, their coming into being could not be conceived. This [comes about] because God is the Truth (al-Haqq), i.e., the established, existing One; and because He is able to bring the dead to life and able over everything that is within His power; and because He is Wise, who does not break His promise. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 8–10:

It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that it refers to Abu Jahl ibn Hisham. It was also said: it was repeated as he repeated other narratives. And it was said:

The first (verse) concerns the followers of blind imitation (muqallidun), and this one concerns the followers of blind imitation. By knowledge ('ilm) is meant necessary knowledge (al-ʿilm al-ḍaruri, knowledge that arises immediately and cannot be doubted). By guidance (huda) is meant inference and reflection (istidlal wa-nazar), because it leads to knowledge. By the illuminating Book is meant revelation; that is, he argues with conjecture and speculation, not with any of these three.

Thaniya al-ʿatf (lit. "bending the side") is an expression for arrogance and self-conceit, like turning the cheek away in disdain (taʿsir al-khadd) and twisting the neck (lawy al-jid). It was also said: it means turning away from the remembrance (dhikr). It is narrated from al-Hasan: thaniya ʿiṭfihi, with a fatha on the ʿayn, meaning: one who withholds his side (māniʿ taʿaṭṭufihi). The phrase liyuḍilla ("so that he may lead astray") is a statement of the purpose of the argumentation. It is read with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and with a fatḥa on it.

If you say: what was his aim in his argument, that he should lead astray from the way of Allah, so how is it given as the reason for it? And was he not also rightly guided, so that when he argued he departed from guidance into error? I say: when his argument led to error, it was made as if it were his aim. And since guidance was presented to him, but he neglected it, turned away from it, and turned to argument in falsehood, he was made as one who has departed from guidance into error.

As for his disgrace (khizyuhu): it is what befell him on the day of Badr of humiliation and killing. The cause of what he was afflicted with of the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter is what his hands had sent forward, and it is the justice of God in punishing the wicked and rewarding the righteous.

It was also said: it means turning away from the remembrance (dhikr). It is narrated from al-Hasan: thaniya ʿiṭfihi, with a fatha on the ʿayn, meaning: one who withholds his side (māniʿ taʿaṭṭufihi). The phrase liyuḍilla ("so that he may lead astray") is a statement of the purpose of the argumentation. It is read with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and with a fatḥa on it.

If you say: what was his aim in his argument, that he should lead astray from the way of Allah, so how is it given as the reason for it? And was he not also rightly guided, so that when he argued he departed from guidance into error? I say: when his argument led to error, it was made as if it were his aim. And since guidance was presented to him, but he neglected it, turned away from it, and turned to argument in falsehood, he was made as one who has departed from guidance into error.

As for his disgrace (khizyuhu): it is what befell him on the day of Badr of humiliation and killing. The cause of what he was afflicted with of the disgrace of this world and the punishment of the Hereafter is what his hands had sent forward, and it is the justice of God in punishing the wicked and rewarding the righteous.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 11–13:

﴿Among mankind is he who worships Allah on an edge (ḥarf). If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial befalls him, he turns back upon his face. He has lost this world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.﴾ — Here, "ʿalā ḥarf" means on an edge (ṭaraf) of the religion, not in its middle or its heart. This is a metaphor for their being in unease and disturbance regarding their religion, not in calm and tranquillity, like one who stands at the edge of an army: if he senses victory and booty, he settles and is at ease; otherwise he flees and runs off in his direction.

It is said: it was revealed concerning some Bedouin Arabs who came to Madina. When one of them was healthy in body, his mare foaled a fine colt, his wife bore a healthy boy, and his wealth and livestock increased, he would say: "I have obtained nothing but good since I entered this religion of mine," and he would be at ease. But if the matter was the opposite, he would say: "I have obtained nothing but evil," and he would turn back.

It is related on the authority of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri that a man from the Jews embraced Islam, then misfortunes befell him, so he regarded Islam as an omen of ill luck, and came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "Release me from it (aqilni)." He said, "Indeed Islam is not to be revoked (inna al-Islam la yuqal)." [[Thus al-Wahidi mentioned it in al-Asbab, but without a chain of narration. Then he said: ʿAṭiyya related from Abu Saʿid, and he mentioned it differently. Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from the narration of ʿAṭiyya from Abu Saʿid, who said: "A man from the Jews embraced Islam, then his wealth and children were lost, and he regarded Islam as an omen of ill luck — the hadith is similar." Its chain is weak. Al-ʿUqayli narrated from the narration of ʿAnbasa ibn Saʿid from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, who said: "A Jew came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and embraced Islam at his hands, then he returned to his home, and he was afflicted in his eye and in his child, so he returned to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'Release me from it' — the hadith." It does not mention the revelation of the verse in it. ʿAnbasa is very weak.]] Then the verse was revealed.

The one afflicted by a trial who does not submit to the decree of Allah and goes out to that which displeases Allah has gathered upon himself two trials: the first is the loss of what he was afflicted with, and the second is the loss of the reward of the patient. So he has lost both worlds. It has been read "khāsir al-dunya wa al-ākhira," in both the accusative and the nominative. The accusative is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and the nominative is as the subject (fāʿil). Placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun is a good usage. Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject. "Al-ḍalāl al-baʿīd" is borrowed from the one who strays far into the wilderness, whose distance of error is long and far-reaching.

If you say: harm and benefit are negated of the idols and affirmed of them in the two verses, and this is a contradiction.

I say: when the meaning is grasped, this misconception disappears. Allah the Exalted mocked the disbelievers by stating that they worship a lifeless object that possesses neither harm nor benefit, while they believe in it, through their ignorance and error, that they gain benefit from it when they seek its intercession. Then He said: on the Day of Resurrection this disbeliever will say, with supplication and crying out, when he sees the harm he has suffered from the idols and his entry into the Fire through worshipping them, and he sees no trace of the intercession he claimed for them: ﴿He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. Surely wretched is the patron and surely wretched is the companion.﴾ Or it is a repetition of "yadʿū" (he calls), as if He said: he calls upon what does not harm him and what does not benefit him, apart from Allah; then He said: "for one whose harm (through being worshipped) is nearer than his benefit (through being an intercessor), surely wretched is the patron." In the reading of ʿAbd Allah it is "man ḍarruhu" without the lam. "Al-mawla" means the helper, and "al-ʿashīr" means the companion, like His saying: ﴿how wretched is the companion (al-qarīn)﴾.

This is a statement that has undergone abridgement. The meaning: God helps His Messenger in this world and the Hereafter. So whoever among his envious and hostile foes thinks that God does otherwise, and hopes for that, and is enraged that he (the Messenger) attains his aim, let him exhaust his capacity and strain his effort to remove what enrages him, by doing what one does when rage reaches its utmost limit, until he stretches a rope to the sky of his house and then chokes himself. Let him look and imagine in his own mind: if he did that, would the victory of God that enrages him go away?

The choking is called "qat'" (cutting) because the one who chokes cuts off his breath by blocking his passages. From this it was said of breathlessness: "al-qat'" (qat' — the cutting), meaning the succession of breath; this is conveyed by al-Sihah (lexicon). (ʿA)

His act is called "kayd" (scheming) because he placed it in the position of scheming, since he had no other option. Or it is by way of mockery, because he did not scheme against the one he envied; rather he schemed against himself. The meaning: what is in his hand is nothing but what does not remove what enrages him.

It was also said: "Let him stretch a rope to the shielding sky, and let him ascend on it, and let him cut off the revelation or descend upon it." It was also said: some Muslims, out of intense rage and fury toward the polytheists, were impatient for the victory God had promised His Messenger, and others among the polytheists wished to follow him and feared that his affair would not be established. So this verse was revealed.

The "victory" has been interpreted as "provision" (rizq). It was also said: its meaning is that provisions are in God's hand; they are not obtained except by His will, and the servant must be content with His apportioning. So whoever thinks that God is not his provider, and has no patience or submission, let him reach the utmost degree of distress, which is choking; for that will not reverse the apportionment nor return the one who has been provided for.

That is: and in the same way [of sending down], We sent down the whole Qur'an as ﴿clear signs﴾, and [that] Allah ﴿guides by it those whom He knows will believe﴾. Or: He makes firm those who have believed and increases them in guidance. He sent it down thus, making it clear.

The separation is absolute, and it may refer to separating them in all states and places, so that He does not requite them with one uniform recompense without any difference, nor gather them in a single station. It has also been said: the religions are five, four belonging to Satan and one to the Most Merciful. The Sabians were placed with the Christians because they are a type of them. It has also been said that ﴿He will separate them﴾ means that He will judge between them, that is, between the believers and the disbelievers. The particle ﴿إِنَّ﴾ (inna) was placed before each of the two parts of the sentence to add emphasis (tawkid).

Similar to this is the verse of Jarir:

Indeed the caliph, indeed God has clothed him
with the garment of kingship, by which the final outcomes are hoped for.

Here, "indeed God has clothed him" is the predicate (khabar) of the first ﴿إِنَّ﴾, and he repeated it to intensify the emphasis. "Clothed him" (sarbalahu) means: He dressed him in kingship, which resembles a garment. It is narrated as "garment of kingship by which" (sarbal mulk bihi), meaning: by that garment or that kingship. "Tuzjā" means: the outcomes are driven along. "Al-khawātīm" is the plural of khātim, pronounced with a fatha or a kasra, and the original form was khawātim, with a yā' added. What is meant by it is the good final outcomes of affairs. Abu Hayyan said: it is possible that the predicate of ﴿إِنَّ﴾ is the phrase "by which is driven," and that the clause "indeed God has clothed him" is a parenthetical (i'tiraD) insertion. It is also narrated as "by which is hoped for" (bihi turjā) with the letter rā', and this needs to be verified.

Its obedience to Him in what happens to it of His acts, and in what He brings upon it of His governance and subjugation of it, is called prostration (*sujud*) to Him. This is a figurative likening of its obedience to the inclusion of the acts of the responsible person under the category of obedience and submission. It is the prostration beyond which every other humbling falls short.

If you say: what do you make of His words ﴿and many of mankind﴾ and what it contains of the two objections? The first is that prostration, in the sense you have explained it, is not performed by some people and not others. The second is that prostration was first ascribed in general terms to whoever is in the earth, of humankind and jinn, and then ascribing it to many of them afterward is a contradiction. I say: I do not treat ﴿many﴾ as a term coordinated with the separate items that fall under the governance of the verb. Rather I put it in the nominative by a suppressed verb that is indicated by His words ﴿prostrates﴾, meaning: and many of mankind prostrate to Him, a prostration of obedience and worship.

I did not say that ﴿prostrates﴾, which is the apparent reading, should be understood in the sense of obedience and worship for these people, because a single word cannot correctly be used in one situation with two different meanings. Or I could make it the subject of a nominal sentence, with the predicate omitted, namely: ﴿deserves punishment﴾, because the predicate of its counterpart indicates it, which is His words ﴿the punishment has become due upon him﴾. It is also permissible to make ﴿of mankind﴾ the predicate of it, meaning: of mankind, those who are mankind in truth, who are the righteous and the God-fearing. It is also permissible to exaggerate the number of those upon whom the punishment is due, so that ﴿many﴾ is conjoined to ﴿many﴾ and then one reports about them that the punishment has become due upon them, as if it were said: many and many of mankind, the punishment has become due upon them.

The reading is ﴿ḥaqq﴾ with a damma (*ḥaqqu*), and it was also read ﴿ḥaqqan﴾ (*ḥaqqan*), meaning: the punishment has become due upon them as a truth.

And whoever God humiliates, by decreeing for him wretchedness because of what preceded in His knowledge of his disbelief or his wickedness, then he remains humiliated, and you will not find for him any honorer. It was read ﴿mukrim﴾ with a fatḥa on the *rāʾ* (*mukram*), meaning honoring.

He ﴿does what He wills﴾ of honoring and humiliating, and He wills of that only what the deeds of the doers and the beliefs of the believers require.

His saying "hādhāni" (هذانِ) is according to the wording (lafẓ), and "ikhtaṣamū" (اخْتَصَمُوا) is according to the meaning (maʿnā), like His saying ﴿And among them are those who listen to you, until when they go out﴾ (47:16). In a narration from al-Kisāʾī it is read "khaṣmān" (خصمان) with a kasra. It has also been read "quṭṭiʿat" (قطعت) with the lightened form.

It is as though God determines for them fires according to the measures of their bodies, enclosing them as garments that are cut out to fit the one who wears them. It is also possible that those fires are layered over each of them, like garments layered one over another on the one who wears them. A similar expression is ﴿their garments of pitch﴾ (14:50). Al-ḥamīm (الحميم) is boiling water. From Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him: "If a single drop of it fell upon the mountains of the world, it would melt them." ﴿Melted (yuṣhar)﴾ means it is melted. It is narrated from al-Ḥasan with the doubled hāʾ (يُصَهَّر) for emphasis, meaning: when the boiling water is poured over their heads, its effect inwardly is like its effect outwardly, so it melts their insides and their intestines just as it melts their skins. This is more emphatic than His saying ﴿and they are given boiling water to drink, which cuts their intestines to pieces﴾ (47:15).

Al-maqāmiʿ (المقامع) are whips. A ḥadīth says: "If a single maul of it were placed on the earth and both jinn and mankind gathered together to lift it, they could not lift it."

[[It is in (the collections of) Aḥmad and Abū Yaʿlā, from the narration of Ibn Lahīʿah from Darrāj. Its wording, in His saying ﴿and for them are maces of iron﴾: "If a mace of it were placed on the earth…" the ḥadīth.]]

and remember when We settled Ibrahim (Abraham) at the site of the House, [saying]: ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House for those who circle it, and those who stand [in prayer], and those who bow and prostrate.﴾ (Qur'an 22:26) — wait, the verse quoted in this passage is only the first part, so I translate the text as it stands:

And remember when We made for Ibrahim the place of the House a ṣabah (ﻣﺒﺎءة, mubā'a), i.e., a place of return to which one returns for building and worship.

The House was raised to the sky at the time of the Flood, and it was of red ruby. So God informed Ibrahim of its place by means of a wind He sent, called al-Khajuj, which swept clean what was around it, and he built it on its old foundation. And "an" here is the explanatory (al-mufassira) "an." If you say: how can the prohibition of associating partners and the command to purify the House be an explanation of "settling" (al-tabwi'a)? I say: the settling was intended for the sake of worship, so it is as if it were said: "We made Ibrahim serve [Us], and We said to him: ﴿Do not associate anything with Me, and purify My House﴾ from idols and images and filth being thrown around it." [[The commentary's note: in the Sihah, "al-wathan" is "al-sanam" (idol). (ʿ)]] The reading "yushrik" with the ya' (third person) is also transmitted.

﴿And proclaim to the people﴾: call out to them. Ibn Muhaysin read it as *wa-ādhan* (وآذن).

The proclamation for the pilgrimage (*hajj*) is that one says: "Perform the pilgrimage," or "It is incumbent upon you to perform the pilgrimage." It is reported that he ascended Abu Qubays and said: "O people, perform the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord." [The editor's note: al-Tha'labi transmitted this from al-Hasan, and his chain to him is at the beginning of the book.]

Al-Hasan said that it is an address to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who was commanded to do this during the Farewell Pilgrimage. [The editor's note: al-Tabari transmitted it from Ibn 'Abbas, with the wording "he stood at the Stone" and in another narration "at his station, and he said: 'O people, perform the pilgrimage to the House of your Lord,' and they answered him: 'Here I am, O Allah, here I am.'"]

﴿On foot﴾: *rijālan* is the plural of *rājil* (pedestrian), like *qā'im* and *qiyām*. It is also read *rujālan* with a damma on the *rā'* and a light or heavy *jīm*, and *rujālī* like *ajālā*, from Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿And upon every lean camel﴾: this is a circumstantial clause coordinated upon the previous circumstantial clause, as if he had said: "on foot and riding." ﴿They will come﴾ (*ya'tīna*) is an attribute of *kull ḍāmir* (every lean camel), because it has the sense of a plural. It is also read *ya'tūna*, as an attribute of the men on foot and the riders.

﴿From every distant pass﴾: *al-'amīq* means distant. Ibn Mas'ud read *mu'īq*. It is said: "a well of great depth" (*bi'r ba'īdat al-'umq wal-ma'q*). [The editor's note: In *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* (of al-Jawhari), *al-ma'q* is the inner depth of a thing, and *al-i'māq* is like *al-a'māq*, referring to what is far off among the remote edges of the deserts.]

Al-Zamakhshari, *al-Kashshaf*, commentary on Surah 22, verse 28:

He left "المنافع" (al-manafi') indefinite, because he intended benefits specific to this worship, both religious and worldly, that are not found in other acts of worship. It is reported from Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, that he used to rank the acts of worship before he performed the Hajj. When he performed it, he placed the Hajj above all other acts of worship, because of the special qualities he witnessed in it. He expressed slaughtering and sacrificing (al-nahr wa al-dhabh) by mentioning the name of God, because the people of Islam do not cease to mention His name when they slaughter or sacrifice. This indicates that the primary purpose in what is offered to draw near to God is that His name be mentioned. The speech has been beautifully embellished by combining His words ﴿that they may mention the name of God﴾ with His words ﴿over what He has provided for them﴾. Had it been said, "that they may slaughter cattle on known days," you would not have seen any of that beauty and splendour.

"الأيام المعلومات" (al-ayyam al-ma'lumat, the known days): according to Abu Hanifa, these are the days of the first ten (of Dhu al-Hijjah). This is also the view of al-Hasan and Qatada. According to his two companions, they are the days of sacrifice (ayyam al-nahr).

"البهيمة" (al-bahimah): it is general to every quadruped on land and sea, and it is specified by "الأنعام" (al-an'am), which are camels, cattle, sheep and goats.

The command to eat from them is a command of permission (ibahah), because the people of the Jahiliyyah used not to eat from their sacrifices. It may also be a recommendation (nadb), because it involves equality with the poor, comforting them, and practising humility. For this reason, the jurists have recommended that a person of means eat about one third of his sacrifice.

It is reported from Ibn Mas'ud that he sent an offering (hadi) and said concerning it: "When you slaughter it, eat, give in charity, and send some of it to Utbah," meaning his son. [[Al-Tabari narrated it through the report of Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Ibrahim, from Alqamah: that Abdullah sent an offering with him and said: "Eat, you and your companions, one third; give in charity one third; and send one third to my brother Utbah." Note: the copies of al-Kashshaf read "يعنى ابنه" (meaning his son), which is a distortion; it is in fact "أخوه" (his brother).]]

In a hadith [[Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, Ahmad and Ishaq narrated it through the report of Khalid al-Hadha', from Abu al-Malih, from Utbah, who said: the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "We used to forbid you from eating the flesh of the sacrifices beyond three days, so that it would suffice you. Now God has brought abundance, so eat, store, and seek reward (wa'tajiru)." This is the wording of Abu Dawud. Muslim, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah do not have "wa'tajiru." Al-Nasa'i, in one narration, has "wa tasaddaqu" (and give in charity), and there is a witness for it from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri according to Ahmad. Benefit: In al-Nihayah, he said: "i'tajiru" means "tasaddaqu," seeking reward. It is not "ittajir" with assimilation (idgham) from trade (tijarah). Al-Harawi permitted the assimilation and cited as evidence the saying "من يتجر مع هذا فيصلى معه" (whoever trades with this one and prays with him). There is no proof in it, since it may be from trade.]]: "Eat, store, and seek reward" [[The saying "وائتجروا" (wa'tajiru): the apparent meaning is that the intent is to seek reward through charity. (Ayn)]].

"الْبائِسَ" (al-ba'is) is the one afflicted by distress (bu's), that is, hardship. "والْفَقِيرَ" (wal-faqir) is the one whom need has weakened.

Provision of the Pilgrimage (qada' al-tafath): trimming the moustache and the nails, plucking the armpit hair, and shaving the pubic hair. Tafath means filth, so the meaning is the removal of filth.

It was also read as "wal-yuwfu" (with the fa' doubled), "nudhurahum": their vows, meaning the obligations of their pilgrimage, or whatever acts of righteousness they might vow during their pilgrimage. "Wal-yattawwafu": the tawaf al-ifadah (the Tawaf of Visitation), which is the tawaf of the Visitation that is one of the pillars of the Hajj, and by which full release from the state of ihram is attained. It was also said: it is the tawaf al-sadr, which is the farewell tawaf. "Al-'Atiq": the ancient, because it is the first House established for mankind, according to al-Hasan. From Qatadah: "more liberated (a'taq) from the tyrants; how many a tyrant set out toward it to demolish it, and God prevented him." From Mujahid: "It was never possessed." From him also: "more liberated from drowning." It was also said: it is a noble House, from their saying "'ataq of horses and birds." If you say: al-Hajjaj did gain power over it, yet it was not protected. I say:

He did not intend to seize the House itself; rather, Ibn al-Zubayr took refuge in it, so he devised a way to expel him, then rebuilt it. When Abraha intended to seize it, God did to him what He did.

That is a preposed subject (*mubtada'*) with an omitted predicate: "the matter and the affair is that," just as a writer presents a section of his book on some point and then, when he wishes to take up another matter, says: "Now, such and such was the case." The *hurma* (sacred thing) is whatever it is not permissible to violate. All that God has obligated with this quality, such as the rites of the Hajj and other things, may be understood in two ways: that it is general across all of His obligations, or that it is specific to what relates to the Hajj. From Zayd ibn Aslam: the sacred things are five: the Sacred House (al-Ka'bah al-Haram), the Sacred Mosque, the Sacred City, the Sacred Month, and the one in the state of ihram until he is released. ﴿That is better for him﴾, meaning: then glorifying them is better for him. The meaning of glorifying is knowing that they must be observed, guarded, and upheld.

"What is recited" is not an exception from the cattle; rather the meaning is ﴿except what is recited to you﴾, that is, the verse declaring its prohibition, which is His saying in Surat al-Ma'idah: ﴿Forbidden to you are carrion and blood﴾. The meaning is: God has permitted you all the cattle except what He excepted in His Book. So guard His limits, and beware of forbidding anything He has made lawful, like the idolaters' prohibition of the *bahirah* and the *sa'ibah* and other things, or of making lawful what God has forbidden, like their permitting the eating of the *mawquudhah* (animal killed by a blow) and carrion and other things.

When He urged the glorification of His sacred things and praised those who glorify them, He followed it with the command to avoid idols and false speech, because the unity of God, denying partners to Him, and truthfulness of speech are the greatest of sacred things and the first in precedence. He combined *shirk* (associating partners with God) and false speech in one connection, because *shirk* is a kind of false speech: the polytheist claims that the idol deserves worship. It is as if He said: "Avoid the worship of idols, which is the head of falsehood, and avoid false speech entirely; do not approach anything of it, given its extreme ugliness and vileness." And consider what a thing of this kind, the worship of idols, is!

He called idols *rijs* (filth), and likewise wine, gambling, and the divining arrows, by way of comparison. The meaning: just as you recoil from filth by your nature and avoid it, so you must recoil from these things with the same recoiling. He alerted to this meaning with His saying ﴿filth from the work of Satan, so avoid it﴾; He made the reason for avoiding it that it is filth, and filth is to be avoided. ﴿From the idols﴾ is an explanation and specification of the filth, like your saying: "I have twenty of the dirhams," because *rijs* is vague, encompassing more than one thing; it is as if it were said: "Avoid the filth, which is the idols."

*Zur* (falsehood) comes from *zawr* and *izwirar*, which means deviation, just as *ifk* (lie) comes from *afakahu*, when one turns it away. It has been said that "the word of falsehood" is their saying: "This is lawful and this is unlawful," and whatever resembles that of their fabrications. It has also been said: it is false testimony. From the Prophet ﷺ: he prayed the dawn prayer, and when he had given the salam he stood up, faced the people with his face, and said: "False testimony has been made equal to *shirk* with God, false testimony has been made equal to *shirk* with God, false testimony has been made equal to *shirk* with God," and then he recited this verse.[[Narrated by Abu Dawud, Ahmad, Ishaq, and Ibn Abi Shaybah, from the narration of Sufyan ibn Ziyad al-'Usfuri from his father, from Habib ibn al-Nu'man, from Hurim ibn Fatik. And al-Tirmidhi narrated it from the narration of al-'Usfuri from Fatik ibn Fudalah from Anas ibn Hurim, thus he said.]]

It has also been said: it is lying and slander. And it has been said: it is the saying of the people of Jahiliyyah in their talbiyah: "Here I am, You have no partner, except a partner who is Yours, You own him and what he owns."

This comparison may be of the compound (*murakkab*) or the separated (*mufarraq*) type. If it is a compound comparison, it is as if He said: whoever associates partners with God has destroyed himself with a destruction that has no end, by depicting his state in the likeness of one who fell from the sky, so that birds snatched him and tore him into pieces in their crops, or the wind blew him violently until it hurled him into some distant abyss. If it is a separated comparison, then faith in its height is likened to the sky, the one who abandoned faith and associated partners with God is likened to the one who fell from the sky, the desires that scatter his thoughts are likened to the snatching birds, and Satan, who hurls him into the valley of error, is likened to the wind that blows what it has seized into some ruinous abysses.

This meaning has been established more fully than this. In establishing it there is a likening of the scattered thoughts of the disbeliever to the snatching birds, and in the likening of Satan's hurling by desire together with the wind into a deep place there is room for examination, because the two matters are mentioned in the context of dividing the state of the disbeliever into two parts. When the first is made a parable for the divergence of desires and thoughts, and the second a parable for the whisperings of Satan, then he has made them one thing, because the scattering of thoughts and the divergence of desires are attributed to the whisperings of Satan, and so the intended division is not realized. What appears in establishing the two comparisons is other than that. We say: since the state of the disbeliever has been divided into two parts with no more beyond them, the first of them is the one who wavers and keeps on in doubt, not resolved upon a single error. This part of the polytheists is likened to one whom birds snatched and scattered, so that no bird seizes a piece of him without another snatching it from it, and that is the state of the one who wavers: no fancy appears to him without his following it and descending from what he was upon. The second is the polytheist resolved upon a false belief; if he were sawn with saws he would not turn back or return. There is no way to make him doubt, and no hope of moving him from what he is upon. He is joyful and delighted in his misguidance. This one is likened, in his fixity in his disbelief, to the settling of the one whom the wind hurled into a low valley, so that he settled there. The likening of him to settling in the deep valley, which is the farthest of hollows from the sky, is parallel to the description of his error as far, in His saying: ﴿They are in far error﴾ and ﴿They have strayed far astray﴾, meaning they were resolved upon their error, so their return to the truth was distant. This is the verification of the two parts, and God knows best.]]

Glorifying the rites (sha'a'ir), which are the offerings, since they are among the landmarks of the Hajj, means that one chooses them to be large in body, beautiful, marked, and of high price, and does not haggle over their purchase. For they used to overpay for three things and disliked haggling over them: the offering (hady), the sacrifice (udhiyya), and the slave (raqaba). Ibn 'Umar related from his father, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he offered a noble she-camel for which he was asked three hundred dinars. He asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to permit him to sell it and buy with its price camels for sacrifice (budn).

He forbade him from that and said: "Rather, offer it." (The discussion of this has already passed in the course of Surat al-Baqara.) The Messenger of Allah ﷺ offered one hundred camels, among them a camel belonging to Abu Jahl with a ring of gold in its nose. [Narrated by Ishaq and al-Bazzar from a hadith of 'Ali. And on this topic there is a report from Jabir who said: "All that he brought was one hundred camels, among them a camel with a ring of silver in its nose," narrated by al-Hakim and al-Tabarani through the narration of Zayd ibn al-Habbab from al-Thawri from Ja'far ibn Muhammad from his father from him. Al-Bukhari said: "This is an error on the part of Zayd. It is rather from al-Thawri from Abu Ishaq from Mujahid as a mursal report." And there has come from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ offered among his offerings a camel which had belonged to Abu Jahl, with a ring of gold on its head, in order to enrage the polytheists," narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Hakim, Abu Ya'la and al-Tabarani.] And Ibn 'Umar would drive the camels adorned with cloth of Qibti (qaba'it) and give their meat and their coverings in charity. He believed that obeying Allah by drawing near to Him through them and offering them to His Glorious House is a great matter that must be upheld and hastened to. "For it is among the piety of hearts" (fa-innaha min taqwa al-qulub), i.e., indeed their glorification is among the deeds of those possessing piety of heart. These genitive phrases were omitted, and the meaning cannot be straight except by supplying them, because there must be a returning pronoun from the conditional to "man" to connect to it. The hearts are mentioned because they are the seats of piety, which when it is firmly established and rooted in them, its effect appears in all the other limbs. "Until a term appointed" (ila ajalin musamma): until they are slaughtered, their meat is given in charity, and some of it is eaten.

Thumma (then) denotes delay in time, so it is borrowed to denote delay in states. The meaning: for you there are many benefits in the offerings, in your worldly life and your religion, and Allah only counts the religious benefits, as He said: ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾. The greatest of these benefits and the farthest-reaching in benefit is: "Their place of sacrifice is at the House" (mahilluha ila al-bayt), i.e., the obligation of slaughtering them; or the time of the obligation of slaughtering them in the sanctuary, reaching to the House, as in His saying: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'ba﴾, and what is meant is slaughtering them in the sacred precinct, which is in the ruling of the House, because the sanctuary is the precinct of the House. Similar to this in breadth is your saying: "We reached the city," when you have only approached it and your journey has connected to its boundaries. It has been said: what is meant by the rites is all the rituals, and "their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House" rejects this.

The hearts are mentioned because they are the seats of piety, which when it is firmly established and rooted in them, its effect appears in all the other limbs. "Until a term appointed" (ila ajalin musamma): until they are slaughtered, their meat is given in charity, and some of it is eaten.

Thumma (then) denotes delay in time, so it is borrowed to denote delay in states. The meaning: for you there are many benefits in the offerings, in your worldly life and your religion, and Allah only counts the religious benefits, as He said: ﴿You desire the goods of this world, but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾. The greatest of these benefits and the farthest-reaching in benefit is: "Their place of sacrifice is at the House" (mahilluha ila al-bayt), i.e., the obligation of slaughtering them; or the time of the obligation of slaughtering them in the sanctuary, reaching to the House, as in His saying: ﴿an offering reaching the Ka'ba﴾, and what is meant is slaughtering them in the sacred precinct, which is in the ruling of the House, because the sanctuary is the precinct of the House. Similar to this in breadth is your saying: "We reached the city," when you have only approached it and your journey has connected to its boundaries. It has been said: what is meant by the rites is all the rituals, and "their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House" rejects this.

Allah prescribed for every community a rite of sacrifice (mansak), that they should slaughter for Him, that is, slaughter seeking nearness to Him, and He made the reason for this that His name, may His names be sanctified, be mentioned over the sacrificial animals. The word mansakan is also read with a fatha and a kasra on the sin. It is a verbal noun in the sense of nusk (rite of worship), while the form with kasra can mean the place (of sacrifice).

So to Him submit (aslimu): that is, make the mention sincere to Him alone, and make it wholly for His sake, pure, without mixing it with any association (shirk).

Al-mukhbitun (the humble): those who are modest and submissive, from al-khabt, which is low-lying land. It is also said: they are those who do not wrong others, and if they are wronged, they do not seek to retaliate.

Al-Hasan read wal-muqimiyas-salat (the ones who establish the prayer) in the accusative, by way of supposing the nun is dropped. Ibn Mas'ud read wal-muqimina as-salat, in the original form.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 36:

*Al-budn* (camels reserved for sacrifice) is the plural of *badanah*, so called for the largeness of its body (*badanuhā*). It refers specifically to camels, but the Messenger of God (ﷺ) also linked cows to camels when he said: "A camel is for seven, and a cow is for seven."[[I have not seen this as a saying traced to the Prophet in these exact words. However, Abu Dawud reported it with the wording "a *jazūr* (slaughtered animal) is for seven," and Muslim and the authors of the Sunan collections reported, through Malik from Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, that he said: "We slaughtered with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) a camel for seven and a cow for seven." There is also a related report from Ibn Mas'ud in al-Tabarani.]] So he placed the cow under the ruling of the camel. Accordingly, in the sacred law the term *badanah* covers both species according to Abu Hanifa and his companions. Otherwise, *al-budn* refers to camels, and the verse indicates this.

Al-Hasan read *wa-l-budn* with two *dammahs* (*wal-budnu*), like *thumr* as the plural of *thamarah*. Ibn Abi Ishaq read it with two *dammahs* and a doubled *nun*, following the pausal form (*lafẓ al-waqf*, the pronunciation used when stopping). It has also been read in the accusative and nominative, like the words of God: ﴿and the moon—We have measured it﴾ (Q. 36:39).

*Min sha'a'ir Allah* means: from among the markers (*a'lam*, signs) of the sacred law that God has prescribed. Attributing them to His name is a way of honouring them. *Lakum fīhā khayr* is like His words: ﴿for you there are benefits in them﴾ (Q. 22:33). It is part of the pilgrim's nature to be eager for something that contains good and benefits, as God testifies.

It is related of one of the early Muslims (*salaf*) that he owned only nine dinars, and with them he bought a sacrificial camel. When he was asked about this, he said: "I heard my Lord say: ﴿for you there is good in them﴾." From Ibn Abbas: "Good in this world and the next." From Ibrahim (al-Nakha'i): "Whoever needs its back may ride it, and whoever needs its milk may drink it."

*Dhikr Allah* (mention of God' s name) means that one says at the time of slaughter: "God is greatest; there is no god but God, and God is greatest; O God, from You and to You."

*Ṣawāffa* (standing in rows) means: standing, having arranged their forelegs and hind legs. It is also read *ṣawāfin*, from *ṣufūn al-faras* (the horse standing), which is when it stands on three legs and raises the fourth on the tip of its hoof, because the sacrificial camel is hobbled on one foreleg, so it stands on three. It is also read *ṣawāfī*, meaning: pure, sincerely for the sake of God's face. From 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd: *ṣawāfinā*, with tanwin in place of the vowel of prolongation (*ḥarf al-iṭlāq*) at pause. From some of them: *ṣawāf*, like the Arab saying *a'ṭi al-qaws bārrihā* ("give the bow to its maker"), with the *yā'* (ي) vowelless.[[His saying "ṣawāf" is perhaps *ṣawāfī*, with sukun. (ʿ)]]

*Wujūb al-junūb* (the falling of their flanks) means: their falling to the ground, from *wajaba al-ḥā'iṭ wujūban* ("the wall fell") when it collapses. *Wajabat al-shams wujūban* means "the sun set." The meaning is: when their flanks have fallen and their *nasā'is* have become still,[[His saying "wa-sakanat nasā'isuhā" (and their *nasā'is* became still): in the Ṣiḥāḥ, *al-nasīsah* and *al-nasīs* mean "stirring up of trouble among people," and *al-nasā'is* are the tale-bearers. Also in it: *al-nasīs* is the remaining of the spirit, and it also says "al-īkāl bayna al-nās" (the stirring up between people), which means spreading discord among them. (ʿ)]] then you may eat from them and feed others from them.

*Al-qani'* is the one who asks, from *qanaʿtu ilayhi* and *kana'tu* when one submits to someone and asks him humbly (*qunūʿan*). *Wa-l-mu'tarr* is the one who approaches without asking, or the *qani'* is the one content with what he has and what is given to him without asking, from *qani'tu qan'an* and *qanā'ah*.

*Al-mu'tarr* is the one who approaches with a request. Al-Hasan read *wal-mu'tarra*. *'Arra*, *'arahu*, *i'tarāhu* and *i'tarrahu* all have the same meaning.

Abu Raja' read *al-qan'*, which means the one who is content and nothing more. It is said: *qani'a fahuwa qan'un wa-qāni'*.

God bestowed His favour upon His servants and sought their praise by subjecting the sacrificial camels to them, in the same manner of subjection that they have seen and known. They take them, submissive and obedient to being taken; they hobble them, holding them with their legs raised, and then they stab them in the chest (*labbān*). Had God not subjected them, they would not have been able to manage them, and we would not be any less capable than some wild animals that are smaller in body and less strong. And what has become a lasting (*yata'abbad*) herd of camels suffices as a witness and a lesson.

Meaning: it is not the flesh of the sacrificial animals that reaches God, nor their blood spilled in slaughter; rather, what is meant is the owners of the flesh and blood. The sense is: those who sacrifice and draw near to their Lord will please Him only by observing the intention (niyyah) and sincerity, and by keeping the conditions of piety (taqwa) in the lawfulness of what they draw near with, along with the other legal safeguards and the commands of scrupulousness (wara'). If they do not observe this, the sacrifice and the drawing near will not avail them, however much of it they do.

It has been read: ﴿لَن تَنَالَ اللَّهَ﴾ ("it will not reach God"), and ﴿وَلَٰكِن تَنَالُهُ﴾ ("but it is taqwa that reaches Him"), with the verb written with ta' and with ya'.

It was said: when the people of the Jahiliyyah slaughtered the camels (al-budn), they would splash the blood around the House (the Ka'bah) and smear it on it. When the Muslims performed the Hajj, they wished to do the same, and this verse was revealed.

He repeated the reminder of the blessing of subjugation, then said: ﴿لِّتُكَبِّرُوا اللَّهَ عَلَىٰ مَا هَدَاكُمْ﴾ ("that you may glorify God for having guided you"), for His markers of religion (a'lam dinih) and the rites of His Hajj, by your saying "Allahu akbar" and "La ilaha illa Allah." So he abbreviated the speech by including the meaning of gratitude (shukr) in the glorifying (takbir), and so it took its construction (ta'diyah).

Al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 38:

He singled out the believers for His repelling (of harm) from them and His support of them, as He said: ﴿Indeed, We surely help Our messengers and those who believe﴾, and He said: ﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be helped﴾, and He said: ﴿And another (favour) you love: help from Allah and a near victory﴾. He made the reason for this that He does not love their opposites, namely the treacherous disbelievers who betray Allah and the Messenger, betray their trusts, and deny the blessings of Allah and belittle them [[His words "and belittle them" mean: they consider them insignificant. (Ea.)]]. As for the one who reads ﴿yudafi'u﴾ (He repels), its meaning is that He exaggerates in repelling (harm) from them, just as one who contends (mughalabah) with another exaggerates in it, because the form of the one who overcomes (al-mughalib) comes stronger and more emphatic.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 39–41:

Permission [to fight] is given (أُذِنَ) and they are fought against (ويُقاتَلُونَ); both have been read in the form of the passive voice (al-mabni lil-fa'il) and the passive voice (al-mabni lil-maf'ul) together. The meaning is: permission was given to them to fight, and the object of permission (al-ma'dhun fihi) is omitted, because "they are fought against" (yuqatalun) indicates it. "Because they were wronged" (بِأَنَّهُمْ ظُلِمُوا): that is, because of their being wronged. They were the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The polytheists of Makkah used to harm them with severe harm, and they would come to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among those who had been beaten and wounded, complaining to him, and he would say to them:

"Be patient, for I have not been commanded to fight," until he emigrated, and then this verse was revealed. It is the first verse in which permission to fight was given after the prohibition against it in some seventy-odd [verses]. [[I have not found it in this form. Al-Wahidi in al-Wasit attributed it to the exegetes. I say: it is derived from hadiths, the closest of which is what Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted through the route of Bukayr ibn Ma'ruf from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, who said: "[Allah's words] Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they were wronged." That was because the polytheists of Makkah used to harm the Muslims in Makkah, so they asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to fight them in Makkah. The Prophet (ﷺ) forbade them from doing so. When the Prophet (ﷺ) went out to Madinah, Allah revealed to him: "Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they were wronged." Al-Tabari mentioned that the Companions, may God be pleased with them, asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) for permission to fight the unbelievers when they saw them and attacked them secretly in Makkah before the Hijrah.]] Then God revealed: ﴿Indeed, God does not love any treacherous ingrate﴾. When they emigrated, [the Makkan polytheists] had seized their property and fought them, so He said: ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against﴾ — the verse.

It is also said: it was revealed concerning a people who went out as emigrants, and the polytheists of Makkah intercepted them, so they were permitted to fight them. The informing that He is able to help them is a promise from Him of victory, coming in the manner of the speech of the mighty; and what preceded of His repelling [harm] from those who believed indicates a similar promise too. "Who have been expelled from their homes without right" (أَنْ يَقُولُوا) is in the genitive position as a substitute (badal) for "right" (ḥaqq): that is, without any cause other than monotheism, which ought to be the cause of acknowledgment and empowerment, not the cause of expulsion and exile. Similar to it is: ﴿Do you resent us only because we believed in God?﴾

﴿God repels some people by means of others﴾: [this means] His manifesting and empowering the Muslims, from among them, against the unbelievers through striving (al-mujahadah). Had it not been for that, the polytheists would have overpowered the adherents of the various religions in their times, and their places of worship, and demolished them, leaving the Christians no churches (biya'), nor their monks hermitages (sawami'), nor the Jews prayer-places (salawat), nor the Muslims mosques. Or the polytheists of the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) would have prevailed over the Muslims and over the People of the Book who were under their protection, and demolished the places of worship of both groups. It is also read as "defence" (difa'). And "would have been demolished" (lahudimat) is read with the lightened form. The church was called "ṣalāt" because prayer is performed in it; it is also said that it is an arabized word whose original in Hebrew is ṣalawtha.

﴿Whoever helps Him﴾: that is, whoever helps His religion and His allies. This is a report from God, the Mighty and Majestic, of the unseen, about what the conduct of the emigrants, may God be pleased with them, would be if He established them in the land and extended to them in this world, and how they would conduct the affairs of religion. It is related from Uthman, may God be pleased with him: "By God, this is praise before trial." He means: God praised them before they had done the good that they did.

They said: in it is evidence for the validity of the authority of the Rightly-Guided Caliphs, because God did not grant empowerment and the execution of command together with just conduct to anyone other than them among the emigrants; there is no share in that for the Helpers (Ansar) or the Freed ones (Tulaqa'). It is related from al-Hasan: "They are the community of Muhammad (ﷺ)." It is also said that "those who" (alladhina) is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "whoever helps Him." The apparent reading is that it is in the genitive, following "those who were expelled." ﴿And to God belongs the final outcome of affairs﴾: that is, its return is to His judgment and decree. In it is an emphasis of what He promised of manifesting His friends and raising their word.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 45:

Every elevated thing that overshadows you, whether the roof of a house, a tent, a canopy, or a vineyard, is called ʿarsh (a trellis or framework). Al-khawi means the fallen, from khawa al-najm (when the star falls). It may also mean the empty, from khawa al-manzil (when the dwelling is emptied of its people). And khawa refers to the belly of a pregnant woman (becoming empty). His words ʿalā ʿurūshihā (upon their trellises) must relate to khāwiyah (fallen), in which case the meaning is that they lie fallen upon their roofs, that is, their roofs collapsed to the ground, and then their walls crumbled and fell on top of the roofs. Or the meaning is that they are fallen or empty while their trellises remain intact and sound. Alternatively, it may be a second predicate after a first, as if it were said: "They are empty, and they are upon their trellises," meaning standing, overlooking their trellises, in the sense that the roofs fell to the ground and came to rest within the walls, while the walls remained standing, so they overlook the fallen roofs. If you ask: what is the grammatical position of the two clauses, namely wahiya ẓālimah (while it is wrongdoing) and fa-hiya khāwiyah (so it is fallen)? I say: the first is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the second has no grammatical position, because it is coordinated with ahlaknāhā (We destroyed it), and this verb has no grammatical position.

al-Ḥasan recited muʿaṭṭalah (abandoned), from aʿṭalahu, meaning ʿaṭṭalahu (to render idle). The sense of muʿaṭṭalah is that it was populated, with water in it and the tools for drawing water present, yet it was abandoned, that is, left without anyone drawing from it, due to the destruction of its people. Al-mashīd means either plastered (with gypsum) or of raised construction. The meaning is: How many a town have We destroyed? And how many a well have We left idle of its drawers? And how many a lofty palace have We emptied of its residents? The mention of that is omitted because muʿaṭṭalah indicates it. In this there is evidence that ʿalā (upon) here means maʿa (with), which is more eloquent.

It is related that this is a well upon which Ṣāliḥ (peace be upon him) alighted with four thousand men of those who believed in him, and God saved them from the punishment. It is in Ḥaḍramawt. It was named thus because Ṣāliḥ died when he arrived there (ḥaḍara). Near the well there is a town called Ḥāḍūrāʾ, which the people of Ṣāliḥ built, and they appointed over themselves Jalhas ibn Jallās. They remained there for a time, then disbelieved and worshipped an idol. God sent to them Ḥanẓalah ibn Ṣafwān as a prophet, and they killed him. So God destroyed them, rendered their well idle, and ruined their palaces.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 46:

It is possible that they did not travel, so they were urged to travel, in order to see the places of destruction (maṣāri‘) of those whom God destroyed for their disbelief, and to witness their traces, so that they might take warning. And it is possible that they did travel and saw that, but did not take warning, so they were treated as if they had not traveled and had not seen.

It was also read as fa-takūna lahum qulūb with the yā' (i.e., yakūna, with the verb in the masculine form), meaning: they would understand what must be understood of monotheism (tawhid), and hear what must be heard of the revelation (wahy).

As for fa-innahā (for indeed it), the pronoun is the pronoun of the matter and the affair (ḍamīr al-sha'n wa'l-qiṣṣa), which may come masculine or feminine. In the reading of Ibn Mas‘ud it is fa-innahu.

It is permissible that it be an ambiguous pronoun (ḍamīr mubham) explained by al-abṣār (the eyes), and in ta‘ma (they become blind) there is a pronoun referring back to it. The meaning is: their eyes are sound and intact, with no blindness in them; rather, blindness is in their hearts. Or, the blindness of the eyes is not counted, as if it were not blindness in comparison with the blindness of the hearts.

If you say: what is the benefit of mentioning "the breasts" (al-ṣudūr)?

I say: what is well known and generally believed is that literal blindness has its place in the sight (al-baṣar), namely that the pupil is struck by something that obliterates its light. Using it for the heart is a metaphor and a figure of speech. So when it was intended to affirm what is contrary to the common belief, namely attributing blindness literally to the hearts and negating it from the eyes, this depiction needed additional specification and added definition, so that it would be established that the place of blindness is the hearts and not the eyes. As when you say: "The sharpness is not in the sword, but in your tongue that is between your jaws." Your phrase "that is between your jaws" confirms what you claimed for your tongue and establishes that the locus of sharpness is precisely that and nothing else, as if you had said: I did not deny sharpness from the sword and attribute it to your tongue by slip or inadvertence on my part, but I deliberately intended precisely that.

He denied their urging for the punishment threatened to them, whether it be hastened or deferred, as if he had said: "Why do they hasten it?" It is as though they assumed that God could be eluded, but that assumption is only valid regarding the promise of one who may break his word. God, exalted and majestic, does not break His promise, and what He has promised will certainly befall them, even if after some time. He, glory be to Him, is forbearing (ḥalīm) and does not hasten. From His forbearance and dignity (waqār), and His regarding long periods as short, is that a single day with Him is like a thousand years [[Maḥmūd said: "This indicates God's forbearance, His dignity, and His regarding a long term as short, so that a single day with Him is like a thousand years." Aḥmad said: Dignity (waqār) combined with forbearance is understood linguistically as stillness, composure of the limbs in the face of alarming events, deliberateness and gravity, and similar qualities, which may not be applied to God except on the basis of revelation. As for the word "dignity" in His saying ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not hope for dignity from God?﴾, it has been interpreted as "greatness," so it is not of this kind. In sum, it depends on a reliable transmission.]] according to your reckoning. It has also been said: God will not break His promise regarding respite and delay. It is also read as "ta'uddūn" (with the ta') and "ya'uddūn" (with the ya'). Then He said: ﴿How many a city, whose people were wrongdoers like you, did I give respite for a while, and then I seized them with punishment, and the return is to Me.﴾

I say: the first clause came as an explanation (badal) of His saying ﴿so how was My denial?﴾, whereas this clause has the same status as the two clauses preceding it that are conjoined with "wa," namely His saying ﴿and God will not break His promise﴾ and ﴿and indeed a day with your Lord is like a thousand years﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 49–51:

It is said: "sa'aytu fi amr fulan" (I strove regarding the affair of so-and-so) when one strives to set it right or to spoil it by one's effort. And "'ajizahu" (he competed with him to make him fail) means he outran him, because each of them seeks to make the other fail to catch up with him; so when one outstrips the other, it is said: "a'jazahu" and "'ajazahu" (he rendered him incapable / outpaced him). The meaning is: they strove against its meaning by corruption, through disparaging it, when they named it "sihr" (magic), "shi'r" (poetry) and "asatir" (fables), and through discouraging people from it, [striving] as those who outrun or compete with it in their own opinion, presuming and hoping that their scheming against Islam would be accomplished for them. If you say: "The analogy would seem to be that it should say: ﴿Innama ana lakum bashirun wa nadhir﴾ (Indeed I am only a bringer of good news and a warner to you)," since the two groups are mentioned after it, I say: the discourse is directed to the polytheists. "Ya ayyuha al-nas" (O mankind) is an address to them, and they are the ones of whom it was said: ﴿Have they not travelled through the earth?﴾, and they were described as seeking to hasten [the punishment]. And "the believers were humbled and their reward [was given] so that they would be enraged."
