**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 52:**

﴿Nor did We send any messenger or prophet before you﴾ is clear proof that the messenger (rasul) and the prophet (nabi) are different. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about the prophets and said: "One hundred and twenty-four thousand." It was then asked, "How many of them were messengers?" He said: "Three hundred and thirteen, a great multitude."[[Ahmad and Ishaq narrated it through Mu'adh ibn Rifa'a from Ali ibn Zayd from al-Qasim from Abu Umama: "Abu Dhar asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): How many prophets are there? He said: Such-and-such." Ali is weak. Ibn Hibban narrated it through Ibrahim ibn Hisham al-Ghassani: my father told us from Hudhayfa, meaning Yahya al-Ghassani, from Abu Idris al-Khawlani from Abu Dhar, and mentioned it in a very long hadith.

Ibn al-Jawzi went too far by listing it among the fabricated (mawdu'at) hadiths and accusing Ibrahim ibn Hisham mentioned above. He was not correct in this, for there is another route which al-Hakim and others narrated through Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Sa'idi from Ibn Jurayj from Ata from Ubayd ibn Umayr from Abu Dhar, in full. Yahya al-Sa'idi is weak, but a ruling of fabrication does not stand with this corroborating route (mutaba'a).]] The difference between them is that a messenger among the prophets is one who, together with a miracle, was given a scripture revealed to him. A prophet who is not a messenger is one to whom no scripture was revealed, but who was commanded to call people to the law (shari'a) of someone before him.

The reason for the revelation of this verse is that when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was turned away by his people, when they opposed him, when his own clan went against him and did not support him in what he brought, he wished, out of his great distress at their aversion and his eagerness and anxiety for their Islam, that nothing be revealed to him that would repel them, hoping that this might serve as a way to win them over and bring them down from their error and obstinacy. This wish persisted in him until surah "The Star" (al-Najm) was revealed to him while he was in the assembly of his people, and that wish was in his own soul. He began to recite it, and when he reached the words ﴿And Manat, the third, the other﴾, Satan cast into his wish what he had wished for, that is, he whispered to him what he had embellished for him, so that his tongue slipped, by way of forgetfulness and error, into saying:

"Those are the exalted cranes (gharaniq al-ula), and their intercession is to be hoped for."[[Al-Bazzar, al-Tabari, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Umayya ibn Khalid from Shu'ba from Abu Bishr from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: "I do not know it except from Ibn Abbas, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was in Makka and recited surah al-Najm until he reached the words of the Exalted: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-Uzza, and Manat, the third, the other?﴾ and there came upon his tongue: 'Those are the exalted cranes, their intercession is to be hoped for.' The idolaters of Makka heard this and rejoiced. The matter became confused for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Nor did We send any messenger or prophet before you but when he wished, Satan cast into his wish...﴾" In the version of Ibn Mardawayh it adds: "When he reached its end, he prostrated, and the Muslims and the idolaters prostrated with him." Al-Tabari narrated it from Sa'id ibn Jubayr as a mursal (a report lacking a companion in its chain). Ibn Mardawayh narrated it from Abu Asim al-Nabil from Uthman ibn al-Aswad from Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas, similarly, and he did not doubt its connection (wasl), and this is the soundest part of this hadith. Al-Bazzar said: Umayya ibn Khalid alone narrated its connection from Shu'ba, while others narrate it from him as a mursal. Al-Tabari and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it by another route from Ibn Abbas, through al-Awfi from his grandfather Ata from him. Al-Tabari also narrated it through Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, through Qatada, and through Abu al-Aliya. These are mursal reports, some of which strengthen one another.

The core of the story is in the Sahih with the wording: "that the Prophet (ﷺ), while in Makka... prostrated, and the Muslims, the idolaters, the jinn and mankind prostrated with him." Al-Bazzar said: What is known for this is the narration of al-Kalbi from Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through that route. al-Waqidi narrated it through another route.

I say: in the totality of these reports there is a refutation of Iyad, who said that those among the exegetes and others who mentioned it did not have any of them support it by a chain, nor trace it back to its source, except the narration of al-Bazzar. Al-Bazzar explained that he knew of no route that may be cited other than what he mentioned, and in it there is what there is, together with the occurrence of doubt. I say: as for its weakness, there is no weakness in it at all, for all of them are trustworthy (thiqat). As for the doubt in it, its effect may appear even if it is a single unusual (gharib) route, but at most it becomes a mursal, which is proof only for Iyad and others who accept the mursal of a trustworthy narrator; as for those who reject the mursal, it is strengthened only by the multiplicity of corroborating routes whose narrators are trustworthy. As for his criticism of it on account of differences in wording, weak and feeble reports have no effect on a strong report. So from the story one relies on the sound narration, that is, one relies on the corroborated narration, and in it and in what corroborates it there is no confusion (idtirab), whereas the confusion is in others. So it suffices, since the narration through al-Kalbi is weak, and what is other than it suffices. As for his criticism of it from the standpoint of meaning, it has many precedents among the sound hadiths which are not taken at face value but are interpreted by a sound interpretation that accords with the principles of the religion.]] Then he was given the protection (ʿisma) and became aware of it, and he was alerted to it. It is also said that Jibril (peace be upon him) alerted him, or that Satan himself spoke those words and made the people hear them. When he prostrated at the end of it, all who were in the assembly prostrated with him, and their hearts were at ease. The allowing of Satan to do this was a trial (mihna) and test from Allah. It increased the hypocrites in doubt and darkness, and the believers in light and certainty.

The meaning is: the messengers and prophets before you were likewise in this condition, that when they wished as you wished, Allah empowered Satan to cast into their wishes what he cast into your wish, willing to test those around them. Allah the Exalted has the right to test His servants with whatever kinds of trial and whatever forms of affliction He wills, so as to multiply the reward of the steadfast and increase the punishment of the wavering.

It is said that tamanna (he wished) means "he recited." He recited:

"The Book of Allah wished, on the first night... (tamanna) Dawud wished for the Zabur over the messengers."[[The explanation of this witness was given earlier in the first volume, page 157, so refer to it if you wish. (Its corrector.)]]

And umniyyatuhu (his wish) means "his recitation." It is also said that "those are the exalted cranes" refers to the angels, that is, they are the intercessors, not the idols.

﴿Then Allah abrogates what Satan casts﴾, that is, He takes it away and nullifies it, ﴿then Allah confirms His verses﴾, that is, He establishes them.

"Those in whose hearts is a disease" refers to the hypocrites and the doubters, and "the hard-hearted" refers to the polytheists and the deniers. "And indeed the wrongdoers" means: and indeed these hypocrites and polytheists. The original would be "and indeed they," but the apparent noun was put in the place of the pronoun, as a judgment against them for wrongdoing. "That it is the truth from your Lord" means: so that they may know that the empowering of Satan to cast (the suggestion) is the truth from your Lord, and wisdom. "And indeed Allah guides those who believe" means: to interpret what is ambiguous in the religion with sound interpretations, and to seek for what is unclear in it the meaning required by the firm principles and the established rules, so that confusion does not befall them, doubt does not overtake them, and their feet do not slip. It has also been said:

It is the day in which there is no good. It is said: "a barren wind" (rih 'aqim) when it does not produce rain and does not fertilize trees. It is related from al-Dahhak that it is the Day of Resurrection, and that the intended "Hour" is its precursors. It is also permissible that "the Hour" and "a barren day" both refer to the Day of Resurrection, as if it were said: "until the Hour comes upon them, or the punishment of its day comes upon them," and "a barren day" was placed in the position of the pronoun.

Naming the beginning by its consequence (tasmiyat al-ibtida' bi-al-jaza', i.e. calling the opening of a passage by its result) is because of the connection between them, in that the one is a cause and the other an effect caused by it, just as they treat a like with a like and an opposite with an opposite because of the connection. If you ask: how does the mention of "the Pardoner, the Forgiving" correspond to this place? I say: the one who retaliates is sent forth by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, against the one who neglects punishment, while pardoning the transgressor, by way of recommendation (tanzih) rather than prohibition (tahrim), is something recommended (mandub), and whoever chooses what is recommended and takes the path of recommendation deserves praise from Allah. When he does not prefer that, and takes his revenge and punishes, and does not heed His saying, "But whoever pardons and makes amends, his reward is with Allah" [42:40], and "And that you pardon is nearer to piety" [2:237], and "But whoever is patient and forgives, that is indeed of the steadfast matters" [42:43], then: "Indeed Allah is Pardoning, Forgiving"; that is, He does not blame him for leaving what He sent him to do. And He guarantees him victory in his second attack, for his neglect of pardon, and His vengeance upon the aggressor against him. It is also permissible that He guarantees him victory over the aggressor, while alluding, along with that, to what was more fitting for him, namely pardon, and hinting at it by mentioning these two attributes. Or the mention of pardon and forgiveness indicates that He is able to punish, for the attribute of pardoning is not applied except to one who is able to do its opposite.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 22, verse 61:

That is, that victory is due to His being capable. Among the signs of His perfect power is that ﴿He causes the night to pass into the day and causes the day to pass into the night﴾, or [it is due to] His being the Creator of the night and the day and the One who directs them. Nothing that occurs in them at the hands of His servants, whether good or evil, transgression or justice, is hidden from Him. And ﴿He is All-Hearing of what they say, All-Seeing of what they do﴾. If you ask: what is the meaning of the one of the two alternating [al-mulawain] entering into the other? I answer: it means bringing the darkness of one into the place of the light of the other by the setting of the sun, and the light of the other into the place of the darkness of the first by its rising, just as a sarab is lit by a lamp and goes dark when it is removed. It was said: it means that one of them increases by what the other loses of hours.

[[His statement "just as a sarab is lit": al-sarab, with a fatha, means a path; al-sarab, with a sukun, means a house in the ground. Reported by al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]

The reading ﴿يَدْعُونَ﴾ is also recited with the letter ta' (تاء) and with the letter ya' (ياء). Al-Yamani recited it [with a passive form]. And ﴿أن ما يدعون﴾ is in the passive form (المبنى للمفعول, al-mabni lil-maf'ul, the passive voice), and the wāw (واو) refers back to ﴿ما﴾ because it carries the sense of "the gods" (الآلهة). That is: this description, of creating the night and the day, encompassing what moves within them, and perceiving every word and deed, is because God is the Truth (الحق), whose divinity is established, and because everything that is invoked as a god besides Him is false in its invocation, and because nothing is higher in rank than Him or greater in dominion.

Read as "mukhdarratan" (green), in the form mafʿalah like "muqbilah" and "musbiʿah," meaning possessed of greenness. If you ask, "Why was it not said 'fa-asbahat'?" and why was it turned to the present-tense form, the answer is that there is a subtle point in it: it conveys the continuance of the effect of the rain from time to time, just as you say, "So-and-so bestowed a favour upon me in such-and-such a year, so I go out in the morning and in the evening thankful to him." Had you said "fariḥt wa-ghadawt" (I rejoiced and went out in the morning), it would not have occupied that position.

If you ask, "Why is it in the nominative (rafʿ) and not in the accusative (naṣb) as the answer to the interrogative?" The answer: had it been in the accusative, it would have given the opposite of the intended purpose, because its meaning is the affirmation of greening; with the accusative it would turn into the negation of greening. An example: you say to your companion, "Do you not see that I have bestowed favours upon you, so that you give thanks?" If you put it in the accusative, you are negating his gratitude and complaining of his neglect of it; if you put it in the nominative, you are affirming his thanks.

This and the like of it is what one who is marked by knowledge should be eager to acquire in the science of i'rab (grammatical analysis), and to honour its people. ﴿Lațīf﴾ (Subtle, All-Pervading): whose knowledge or grace reaches every thing; ﴿Khabīr﴾ (All-Aware): well-acquainted with the interests and benefits of creation.

This is a prohibition addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: do not heed their words, and do not allow them to dispute with you. Or it is a rebuke to them for confronting the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with disputation over the religion, while they are ignorant and have no knowledge, and they are the disbelievers of Khuza'ah. It is related that Budayl ibn Warqa' and Bishr ibn Sufyan of Khuza'ah, and others, said to the Muslims: "What is the matter with you, that you eat what you kill, but do not eat what Allah kills?" They meant carrion. Al-Zajjaj said: it is a prohibition to him (ﷺ) from disputing with them, as you say: "So-and-so will not harm you," meaning: "Do not harm him." This is permissible in an action that can only occur between two parties. "In the matter" refers to the matter of religion. It was also said: "in the matter of the rites of sacrifice." It is also read: "fa-la yunaza'annaka," meaning: remain firm in your religion with a firmness such that they do not hope to draw you away to remove you from it. The intent is to increase the steadfastness of the Prophet (ﷺ) by that which stirs his zeal and kindles his anger for Allah and for His religion.

From this is His saying: ﴿And let them not turn you away from the signs of Allah, and do not be among the polytheists, and do not be a supporter of the disbelievers.﴾ Far is it that the aspiration of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would graze around that sanctuary, but it comes in the manner I have told you, of stirring and kindling. Al-Zajjaj said: it derives from "nazaʻtuhu fa-nazaʻtuhu, anzaʻuhu," meaning: I overcame him, i.e., "let them not overcome you in the dispute." If you ask: why did the counterpart of this verse come conjoined with the wāw, while this one has been stripped of it? I say: because that one occurs with what is near to it and suitable to it of the verses concerning the rites of sacrifice, so it was conjoined with its sisters. But this one occurs with verses far from its meaning, so it found no conjunction.

Meaning: even if they insist, out of their obstinacy, on nothing but disputation after you have exerted yourself so that there be no quarrel between you and them, then repel them by saying that God knows best your deeds, their ugliness, and the recompense you deserve for them, so He will requite you for them. This is a warning and an admonition, but delivered gently and mildly.

God decides between you (on the Day of Resurrection), that is, He separates you by reward and punishment. It is also a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he suffered from them. How could what they do be hidden from Him? It is well known among the scholars of God that He knows everything that occurs in the heavens and the earth, and He wrote it on the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh) before it happened.

Encompassing all of that, establishing it, and preserving it is easy for Him, because the Knowing Essence (al-'alim al-dhat) is not prevented from, nor does anything hinder, the connection to a known object. They worship that for which they have held fast to no heavenly proof, in its validity as worship, from the direction of revelation and transmitted report; nor has any necessary knowledge compelled them to it, nor has any rational proof driven them toward it. And for those who have committed such wrongdoing there is no helper who will support them or confirm their position.

the disgusting evil (al-munkar al-fazi'), of scowling and frowning [[His saying "al-tajahhum wa'l-basur": each of them means a contortion of the face. Cited from al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]. Or it is "al-inkar" (denial/disapproval), like "al-mukram" meaning "al-ikram" (honouring). It is also read "yuʿrafu" (they recognise), and "al-munkar". "Al-saṭw" means leaping upon and seizing violently.

It is read "al-nāru" in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, as if a questioner had asked, "What is it?" and it was answered, "The Fire," i.e., "It is the Fire." And in the accusative, as a particularization (ikhtiṣāṣ).

And in the genitive, as an apposition (badal) to "bi-sharrin min dhālikum" (something worse than that), namely from your rage against those who recite (the verses) and your violence against them; or from the displeasure and vexation that has befallen you because of what is recited to you.

"Waʿadahā Allāhu" (God has promised it) is a resumption of speech (istiʾnāf). It is possible that "al-nāru" is the subject (mubtada') and "waʿadahā" the predicate (khabar), and that it is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to it when you put it in the accusative or genitive, with "qad" implied.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (*al-Kashshaf*) on surah 22, verse 73:**

If you ask: what was brought is not a *mathal* (parable), so how did He call it a *mathal*? I answer: a description or a striking story that is received with approval and wonder has been called a *mathal*, by likening it to some of the well-known proverbs (*amthal al-musayyara*), since it is approved and wondrous to them. It is read as *tadʿūna* with both the *tāʾ* and the *yāʾ*, and *yudʿawna* in the passive. *Lan* (لَنْ) is a sister of *lā* in negating the future, except that *lan* negates it emphatically, and its emphasis here serves to show (*al-dalāla*)¹ that the creation of a fly by them is impossible and contrary to their condition, as if He had said: "It is impossible that they should create." If you ask: what is the position (*maḥall*) of ﴿وَلَوِ اجْتَمَعُوا لَهُ﴾? I answer: it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), as if He had said: "It is impossible that they create a fly, even on the condition that they all gather together to create it and cooperate in it." This is among the most eloquent of what God has sent down to expose the ignorance of the Quraysh and the feebleness of their minds, and a testimony that Satan has led them by his halters (*khazamahum bi-khazāʾimihi*)², in that they described as divine, a status which requires power over all things and comprehensive knowledge of all things to their ends, idols and images which are incapable of creating even the least, most despised, most humble and most insignificant of what He created, even if they gathered together and supported one another for that purpose. And more indicative of their impotence and the absence of their power is that, if this least and most despised creature were to snatch something from them, they would gather together to retrieve it from it and would not be able to do so. His saying ﴿ضَعُفَ الطَّالِبُ وَالْمَطْلُوبُ﴾ is like equating them with the fly in weakness. But if you examine it closely, you will find the seeker (*ṭālib*) weaker and weaker still, because the fly is an animate creature while they are inanimate, and the fly is the victor while they are the vanquished. And it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbās that they used to smear the idols with saffron, put honey on their heads, and lock the doors upon them, whereupon the flies would enter through the windows and eat it.

¹ His words "al-dalāla" are perhaps "li-l-dalāla", as in the wording of al-Nasafi. (ʿ)

² His words "inna al-shayṭāna qad khazamahum bi-khazāʾimihi": in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ*, *khazamtu al-baʿīra bi-l-khizāma*, which is a ring of hair placed in the cartilage of a camel's nose, through which the rope is tied. (ʿ)

This is the commentary on Qur'an 22:74, which reads ﴿They have not esteemed God with the esteem due to Him﴾.

"They have not esteemed God with the esteem due to Him" means: they did not know Him with the knowledge that is due to Him, so that they would not give His name to one who is stripped entirely of His attributes, nor deem fit for worship one who is not worthy of it, nor take him as a partner to Him. Indeed, ﴿God is Strong, Mighty﴾; so how could one who is weak and overpowered be taken as a likeness to Him?

This is a refutation of what they denied, namely that the Messenger should be from among humankind, and a clarification that the messengers of God are of two kinds: angels and humans. Then he mentioned that He, exalted is He, is the All-Perceiving of perceptible things, knowing the circumstances of those accountable, what has passed of them and what has remained, not one of them concealed from Him. To Him all matters return, and He who has these attributes is not questioned about what He does, and no one has the right to object to His judgment, His arrangements, or His choice of messengers.

Remembrance (dhikr) has a status that no other act of obedience has. This surah contains indications of that. For this reason He first called the believers to prayer (salah), which is pure remembrance, then to worship other than prayer, such as fasting, pilgrimage (hajj) and fighting in the way of God (ghazw), and then He generalized by urging them to all other good deeds. It has been said: when people first embraced Islam, they used to prostrate without bowing and bow without prostrating, so they were commanded that their prayer be with bowing and prostration. It has also been said that the meaning of "and worship your Lord" (وَاعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمْ) is: direct your bowing and prostration toward the Face of God. Regarding Ibn 'Abbas's interpretation of His words "and do good" (وَافْعَلُوا الْخَيْرَ): it means maintaining ties of kinship and noble character. "So that you may prosper" (لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ) means: do all of this while hoping for success and aspiring to it, without being certain of it, and do not rely on your deeds. On the authority of 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir (may God be pleased with him), who said: I said, "O Messenger of God, does Surah al-Hajj contain two prostrations?" He said: "Yes, if you do not prostrate in them, then do not recite them." [[I have not seen it in this form addressed directly. It was narrated by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ahmad, al-Daraqutni, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, all through the narration of Ibn Lahi'ah from Faraj ibn Mahan from 'Uqbah, with the wording "and whoever does not prostrate in them, let him not recite them." al-Tirmidhi said: its chain is not strong.]] And on the authority of Abdullah ibn Umar (may God be pleased with them both), who said: Surah al-Hajj was given preference by two prostrations. On this basis al-Shafi'i (may God be pleased with him) argued, and he held that there are two prostrations in Surah al-Hajj. Abu Hanifa and his companions (may God be pleased with them) hold that there is only one prostration in it, because they say: the prostration is coupled with bowing (ruku'), which indicates that it is a prostration of prayer and not a prostration of recitation.

And strive (jahadu) in God's cause: an command to go on military campaigns and to struggle against the self and its desires, which is the greater struggle (al-jihad al-akbar). It is reported from the Prophet ﷺ that he returned from one of his campaigns and said: "We have returned from the lesser struggle (al-jihad al-asghar) to the greater struggle (al-jihad al-akbar)." [[Al-Tha'labi reported it like this without an isnad (chain of transmission). Al-Bayhaqi reported it in al-Zuhd from the hadith of Jabir, who said: "A group of warriors came to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He said: 'You have come with the best arrival from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle.' It was asked: 'And what is the greater struggle?' He said: 'The servant's struggle against his desire.'" [The author] said: "It is weak." I say: It comes through the narration of Isa ibn Ibrahim from Yahya ibn Ya'la from Layth ibn Abi Sulaym, and all three are weak. Al-Nasa'i mentioned it in al-Kuna as a statement of Ibrahim ibn Abi Abla, one of the Successors (tabi'un) from the people of Syria.]] "In God's cause," meaning in His essence and for His sake. It is said: "He is a true scholar (haqq 'alim) and a diligent scholar (jadd 'alim)," meaning truly a scholar and certainly a scholar.

From the same usage is ﴿with truly due striving﴾ (haqqa jihadihi). If you ask: what is the point of this idafa (genitive construction), when the expected form would be "its due striving" or "your due striving in it," as in His words ﴿And strive in God's cause﴾? I answer: the idafa can be used with the slightest connection and association. Since striving is specifically connected to God, in that it is done for His sake and for His purpose, its idafa to Him is correct. It is also permissible to extend the adverbial usage, as in the line:

"And a day we witnessed it, Sulaym and 'Amir."

﴿He has chosen you﴾ (ijtaba-kum): He chose you for His religion and for supporting it. ﴿And He has not placed upon you in the religion any hardship﴾: He opened the door of repentance for sinners, and made it wide with kinds of concessions, expiations, blood-money and compensations. Similar to it is His saying, ﴿God intends for you ease and does not intend for you hardship﴾ (2:185). The community of Muhammad ﷺ is the merciful community, marked with this in the earlier scriptures.

The word "religion" (millah) in the accusative is governed by what precedes it. It is as if it were said: "He widened your religion with the widening of your father's religion," then the genitive noun was omitted and the genitive complement put in its place. Or it is in the accusative of specification, meaning: "I mean by the religion the religion of your father," like your saying: "Praise belongs to God, the Praiseworthy." If you ask: Ibrahim was not the father of the whole community? I answer: He was the father of the Messenger of God ﷺ, so he was the father of his community, because the Messenger's community is in the position of his children. ﴿He named you﴾ refers to God Most High. It was also said that it refers to Ibrahim. The first opinion is supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Ka'b: "God named you," ﴿before﴾ (min qabl), meaning before the Qur'an, in the other scriptures, and ﴿in this﴾, meaning in the Qur'an. That is, He preferred you over the nations and named you with this most honorable name, ﴿so that the Messenger may be a witness over you﴾, that he has conveyed to you, ﴿and that you may be witnesses over the people﴾, that the messengers have conveyed to them. Since He has singled you out with this honor and preference, worship Him, trust in Him, and do not seek support or guardianship except from Him, for He is the best protector and helper.

From the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surat al-Hajj, he will be given a reward like the pilgrimage he performed and the minor pilgrimage (umrah) he performed, equal to the number of those who made pilgrimage and minor pilgrimage in the past and in the future." [[Reported by al-Tha'labi and Ibn Mardawayh from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, with the isnad mentioned in Surat Al 'Imran.]]
